## Step 1: fit both models

All imports for this file in one cell.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from great_tables import GT
from plotnine import aes, geom_hline, geom_point, geom_qq, geom_qq_line, geom_smooth, ggplot, labs
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan, linear_reset
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson, jarque_bera
```

```{python}
choc = pl.read_csv("../../data/legacy/chocolate_dataset.csv")
df = choc.to_pandas()

lin = smf.ols("sales ~ price1 + feature1 + display1 + temp + december", data=df).fit()
ll = smf.ols("np.log(sales) ~ np.log(price1) + np.log(price2) + np.log(price3)"
             " + np.log(price4) + feature1 + display1 + temp + december", data=df).fit()
print(f"linear: price1 {lin.params['price1']:.1f}, R² {lin.rsquared:.3f}")
print(f"log-log: elasticity {ll.params['np.log(price1)']:.2f}, R² {ll.rsquared:.3f}")
```

The two R² cannot be compared: one model explains sales, the other log sales.

## Step 2: look at the residuals

```{python}
df["fit"], df["res"] = lin.fittedvalues, lin.resid
(ggplot(df, aes("fit", "res"))
 + geom_point()
 + geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed")
 + labs(x="Fitted sales", y="Residuals", title="Linear model"))
```

```{python}
df["z"] = (df["res"] - df["res"].mean()) / df["res"].std()
(ggplot(df, aes(sample="z"))
 + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
 + labs(x="Normal quantiles", y="Standardised residuals", title="Linear model"))
```

The same two plots for the log-log model:

```{python}
df["fit_ll"], df["res_ll"] = ll.fittedvalues, ll.resid
(ggplot(df, aes("fit_ll", "res_ll"))
 + geom_point()
 + geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed")
 + labs(x="Fitted log sales", y="Residuals", title="Log-log model"))
```

```{python}
df["z_ll"] = (df["res_ll"] - df["res_ll"].mean()) / df["res_ll"].std()
(ggplot(df, aes(sample="z_ll"))
 + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
 + labs(x="Normal quantiles", y="Standardised residuals", title="Log-log model"))
```

## Step 3: test the assumptions

Every test: H0 = the assumption holds; a p-value below 0.05 means a problem.

```{python}
def scorecard(m):
    X = m.model.exog
    return [linear_reset(m, power=2, use_f=True).pvalue, het_breuschpagan(m.resid, X)[1],
            jarque_bera(m.resid)[1], stats.shapiro(m.resid).pvalue,
            max(variance_inflation_factor(X, i) for i in range(1, X.shape[1])), durbin_watson(m.resid)]

tests = pl.DataFrame({"test": ["RESET p", "Breusch-Pagan p", "Jarque-Bera p", "Shapiro-Wilk p", "largest VIF",
                               "Durbin-Watson"],
                      "linear": scorecard(lin), "log-log": scorecard(ll)})
GT(tests).fmt_number(columns=["linear", "log-log"], decimals=3)
```

Robust standard errors, if the funnel stays (HC3), and for autocorrelation (HAC; Session 4 models it properly):

```{python}
hc3 = lin.model.fit(cov_type="HC3")
hac = ll.model.fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 1})
print(f"linear, se of price1: usual {lin.bse['price1']:.1f}, HC3 {hc3.bse['price1']:.1f}")
print(f"log-log, se of the elasticity: usual {ll.bse['np.log(price1)']:.3f}, HAC {hac.bse['np.log(price1)']:.3f}")
```

Influential weeks: Cook's distance, flagged above 4/n.

```{python}
cooks = ll.get_influence().cooks_distance[0]
flag = (choc.with_columns(pl.Series("cooks", cooks))
        .filter(pl.col("cooks") > 4 / choc.height)
        .sort("cooks", descending=True)
        .select("week", "cooks", "price1", "feature1", "display1", "sales"))
flag
```

## Step 4: dummies from a category

```{python}
choc = choc.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("temp") < 5).then(pl.lit("cold"))
    .when(pl.col("temp") < 15).then(pl.lit("mild"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("warm")).alias("season"))
choc["season"].value_counts().sort("season")
```

`C()` turns the category into k − 1 dummies; `Treatment("mild")` makes mild the reference.

```{python}
df = choc.to_pandas()
sea = smf.ols("np.log(sales) ~ np.log(price1) + np.log(price2) + np.log(price3) + np.log(price4)"
              " + feature1 + display1 + december + C(season, Treatment('mild'))", data=df).fit()
dummies = [k for k in sea.params.index if "season" in k or k == "december"]
pl.DataFrame({"dummy": dummies,
              "b": [sea.params[k] for k in dummies],
              "per_cent": [100 * (np.exp(sea.params[k]) - 1) for k in dummies],
              "p": [sea.pvalues[k] for k in dummies]})
```

The 0/1 columns themselves, for a look (never all three in a model with an intercept: the dummy trap):

```{python}
choc.select("week", "temp", "season").with_columns(choc["season"].to_dummies()).head(6)
```

How many 1s does a dummy have? Count before you trust it:

```{python}
choc.select((pl.col("display1") > 0).sum().alias("display_weeks"),
            pl.col("december").sum().alias("december_weeks"),
            pl.col("easter").sum().alias("easter_weeks"))
```

## Step 5: a curve and its turning point

```{python}
quad = smf.ols("sales ~ price1 + I(price1**2)", data=df).fit()
b1, b2 = quad.params["price1"], quad.params["I(price1 ** 2)"]
turn = -b1 / (2 * b2)
print(f"turning point {turn:.2f} EUR; prices in the data {choc['price1'].min():.2f} to {choc['price1'].max():.2f}")
for p in (1.00, 1.25, 1.50):
    print(f"at {p:.2f} EUR, 10 cents more: {(b1 + 2 * b2 * p) / 10:.0f} units")
print(f"RESET p {linear_reset(quad, power=2, use_f=True).pvalue:.4f}")
```

```{python}
(ggplot(choc, aes("price1", "sales"))
 + geom_point()
 + geom_smooth(method="lm", formula="y ~ x + I(x**2)")
 + labs(x="Price of brand 1", y="Weekly sales", title="Quadratic fit"))
```
